title: 6.6 — Heteroscedasticity and Generalized Least Squares (GLS)
breadcrumb: Unit VI → Regression and linear models → 6.6 Heteroscedasticity and GLS
engineName: Diagnose non-constant error variance, understand consequences for OLS inference, and derive and apply feasible generalized least squares.
objectives: Define heteroscedasticity through the conditional error variance.
Distinguish unbiasedness of OLS coefficients from efficiency and validity of conventional standard errors.
Recognize the limits of residual plots and formal heteroscedasticity tests.
Derive the weighted least squares transformation for known unequal variances.
Explain feasible GLS when the variance structure is estimated.
Choose robust standard errors or WLS/FGLS according to the inferential or modelling objective.

prereq.name: Classical linear regression assumptions
prereq.why: The conditional mean and variance of the disturbance determine OLS properties.

prereq.name: OLS estimator and covariance matrix
prereq.why: The variance formula shows exactly where a non-spherical error covariance enters.

prereq.name: Matrix algebra and weighted least squares
prereq.why: GLS is OLS after premultiplying by a suitable whitening transformation.

traps: Heteroscedasticity means Var(uᵢ|X)=σᵢ² is not constant across observations; it does not mean the conditional mean is nonzero.
Under exogeneity and a correctly specified conditional mean, OLS can remain unbiased/consistent despite heteroscedasticity.
Conventional homoscedastic OLS standard errors are generally incorrect; the direction of error is not universally upward.
OLS is generally inefficient among linear unbiased estimators when the covariance matrix is non-spherical.
White/heteroscedasticity-robust standard errors change estimated uncertainty, not the OLS coefficient estimates.
If Ω is known and positive definite, GLS uses Ω⁻¹; WLS is the diagonal special case.
For Var(uᵢ|X)=σ²hᵢ, WLS weights are proportional to 1/hᵢ, not 1/σᵢ.
FGLS substitutes an estimated covariance structure and therefore adds estimation uncertainty; it is not automatically superior in small samples.
Breusch–Pagan tests a specified variance relation; White's test is more general but can consume degrees of freedom.
Do not confuse heteroscedasticity with autocorrelation: one concerns unequal variances, the other cross-observation covariance.
howto: Start by stating the conditional mean and variance assumptions. If the mean model is exogenous but variance is non-constant, OLS coefficients may remain valid while conventional standard errors fail. Use heteroscedasticity-robust inference when the mean model is the target and variance structure is unknown. If a credible variance model is available, transform by its inverse standard deviation and estimate by WLS; with an estimated variance model, call it FGLS and check sensitivity.

sheet: Homoscedasticity: Var(uᵢ|X)=σ²; heteroscedasticity: Var(uᵢ|X)=σᵢ² varies with i.
With exogeneity, heteroscedasticity alone need not bias OLS coefficients.
Conventional OLS standard errors rely on the homoscedastic covariance assumption and may be wrong.
Under heteroscedasticity, OLS is generally not BLUE; it can remain unbiased/consistent.
Robust (sandwich) SEs change inference, not OLS coefficients.
If Ω=σ²H, use H⁻¹; the common scale σ² cancels.
Diagonal H=diag(hᵢ): WLS weights are 1/hᵢ, or transform each row by 1/√hᵢ.
FGLS estimates H (or Ω) before applying GLS.
Breusch–Pagan and White tests assess heteroscedasticity; diagnose with plots and context too.
tricks: If the question asks about coefficient bias, check exogeneity before blaming heteroscedasticity.
If it asks about standard errors, distinguish conventional from robust/sandwich estimates.
For WLS, inverse variance is the weight; inverse standard deviation is the row multiplier.
If Ω=σ²H, the unknown common σ² factor cancels from the GLS coefficient formula.
shortcuts: Unequal variance → conventional SE problem; robust SE is a common inference fix.
Known variance pattern → WLS/GLS can improve efficiency.
Estimated variance pattern → FGLS; report the modelling assumption.
remember: Robust SEs do not repair omitted variables, endogeneity or a misspecified conditional mean.
Finite-sample performance of FGLS depends on how well the variance structure is estimated.

scenes.title: Rebuild the error assumptions
scenes.objective: Recall what the regression disturbance assumptions say.
body: Write the model as yᵢ=xᵢ′β+uᵢ. The conditional mean assumption E(uᵢ|X)=0 says the regressors do not systematically predict the error.
A separate assumption concerns conditional variance. Homoscedasticity says Var(uᵢ|X)=σ² for every observation. Heteroscedasticity allows Var(uᵢ|X)=σᵢ² to vary with i.
These assumptions do different jobs: the mean condition protects coefficient interpretation, while the variance condition enters the covariance matrix and standard errors.

items.recall: The conditional mean of the error is zero.
refresh: It says that after conditioning on the regressors, the error has no systematic average component.
It is central to unbiasedness/consistency arguments for OLS.
It is not the same as saying every realised error equals zero.
The conditional error variance is the same number for every observation after conditioning on X.
Write this as Var(uᵢ|X)=σ², where σ² does not depend on i or the regressor values.
It is a restriction on the spread of the error distribution, not on its centre.
Constant variance is stronger than zero conditional mean; one assumption does not imply the other.

items.recall: The conditional error variance depends on the observation or regressors.
refresh: Some observations can have more variable errors than others.
The variance need not increase monotonically with a regressor.
The key is non-constant conditional variance, not a nonzero conditional mean.

ask.q: Which assumption is directly violated by heteroscedasticity?

scenes.title: Same mean model, different spread
body: Imagine household expenditure explained by income. The average relationship may be correctly specified, but prediction errors can be tightly clustered for low-income households and widely spread for high-income households.
That fan-shaped spread is a visual clue, not a proof. Heteroscedasticity can have many shapes, and a plot can miss patterns that a formal test or subject-matter reasoning detects.

scenario.teaser: Residual spread widens with fitted value
scenario.title: A fan-shaped residual plot
body: A residual-versus-fitted plot shows small vertical spread at low fitted values and much larger spread at high fitted values.
The pattern suggests non-constant conditional variance. It does not by itself identify the exact variance function or prove the cause.
A residual plot is usually examined after fitting the mean model, because fitted values provide a compact summary of the regressors for this diagnostic.
If the widening spread is systematic, conventional homoscedastic standard errors should not be trusted without further adjustment.
Possible next steps include robust standard errors for inference or a defensible model for the conditional variance.
scenario.q: What assumption is the fan shape warning about?
scenario.answer: Constant conditional error variance; the pattern suggests heteroscedasticity.

ask.q: Does a fan-shaped residual plot prove heteroscedasticity?
ask.nudge: A diagnostic plot is evidence, not a formal proof.

scenes.title: Visualise unequal error variance
scenes.objective: Connect variance changes to residual spread.
body: The key feature is changing vertical spread as fitted values or a predictor changes. The conditional centre may remain around zero while the spread changes.
A pattern in spread is distinct from a curved mean pattern. If the residual centre bends, investigate mean-model misspecification as well as variance.

viz.caption: A changing vertical spread around a zero conditional mean is the visual signature to investigate.

scenario.teaser: The centre stays near zero but the spread changes
scenario.title: Variance changes without a mean shift
body: At each value of x, residuals remain centred around zero. Their dispersion, however, increases with x.
This illustrates how E(u|X)=0 can hold while Var(u|X) is non-constant.
This distinction matters in applications where larger units naturally have more variable outcomes, such as expenditure, firm size or production.
A variance-stabilising transformation may sometimes help, but it changes the scale and interpretation of the model and should not be applied mechanically.
The diagnostic question is whether the conditional variance is stable after accounting for the chosen mean model.
scenario.q: Can zero conditional mean coexist with heteroscedasticity?
scenario.answer: Yes. The conditional mean can remain zero while the conditional variance changes.

ask.q: Which residual-plot feature signals changing variance?
ask.nudge: Focus on the width of the vertical cloud.

scenes.title: Consequences for OLS
scenes.objective: Separate coefficient properties, efficiency and inference.

blocks.p: If E(u|X)=0 and the conditional mean model is correctly specified, heteroscedasticity alone does not generally make OLS coefficients biased. Under standard regularity conditions, OLS can remain consistent.

The usual Gauss–Markov covariance condition is Var(u|X)=σ²I. When the covariance is not spherical, OLS is generally not the best linear unbiased estimator; a correctly weighted estimator can be more efficient.
The conventional covariance estimate σ̂²(X′X)⁻¹ is generally invalid under heteroscedasticity. Its error can be upward or downward, so ordinary t and F inference may be unreliable.

nodes.label: Use robust inference or model variance

ask.q: Does heteroscedasticity alone necessarily bias OLS coefficients?
ask.nudge: Keep the zero conditional mean assumption separate from constant variance.

scenes.title: Worked example: diagnose the claim
scenes.objective: Identify which OLS statements remain valid.
scenes.problem: A model satisfies E(u|X)=0 but Var(uᵢ|X)=σ²xᵢ², with xᵢ>0. What follows?

steps.say: The conditional mean restriction is still satisfied.
steps.why: This is the condition supporting the usual OLS unbiasedness argument.

steps.say: The variance is not constant when xᵢ varies.
steps.why: The conditional variance changes with xᵢ, so the errors are heteroscedastic.

steps.say: Do not use the usual homoscedastic standard-error formula without correction.
steps.why: The covariance structure assumed by conventional OLS standard errors is violated.

steps.say: OLS coefficients can remain unbiased, but conventional inference can fail.
steps.why: The variance assumption affects efficiency and estimated uncertainty, not automatically the conditional mean.

ask.q: Which statement is the safest conclusion?
ask.nudge: State the coefficient and standard-error consequences separately.

scenes.title: Detecting heteroscedasticity
scenes.objective: Use graphical and formal diagnostics carefully.

blocks.p: Plot residuals against fitted values and important regressors. Look for changing spread, clusters or other structure. A plot is a diagnostic aid, not a verdict.

A common form regresses squared OLS residuals on selected explanatory variables. The null is constant variance relative to the specified auxiliary variance model. The LM statistic is asymptotically chi-square with degrees of freedom equal to the number of tested slope restrictions.

The White test uses a more general auxiliary regression, often including regressors, their squares and cross-products. It is flexible but can use many degrees of freedom, especially with many regressors.

ask.q: What is the null hypothesis in a standard heteroscedasticity test?

scenes.title: Worked example: Breusch–Pagan LM statistic
scenes.objective: Calculate and interpret a simple BP test statistic.
scenes.problem: An auxiliary regression of squared residuals on two non-constant terms gives n=80 and R²_aux=0.12. Calculate the LM statistic and state its asymptotic reference distribution.

steps.say: Use the LM form n times the auxiliary R-squared.
steps.why: This is the standard large-sample Breusch–Pagan LM statistic.
The sample size multiplies the auxiliary regression R-squared.

steps.say: Use two degrees of freedom for the two tested slopes.
steps.why: The degrees of freedom equal the number of non-constant variance terms being tested.

steps.say: Compare 9.6 with the chosen chi-square critical value or p-value.
steps.why: At the 5% level, 9.6 exceeds 5.991, so reject the constant-variance null in this example.

scenes.title: Choose the response to the problem
scenes.objective: Match robust inference and variance modelling to the objective.
scenes.intro: There is no single automatic repair. Choose according to whether the aim is valid inference for the conditional mean or efficient estimation under a credible variance model.

items.q: What do heteroscedasticity-robust standard errors change?
items.a: The estimated covariance matrix and standard errors, not the OLS coefficient estimates.
When a credible variance/covariance structure is known or can be modelled well.
It estimates the unknown variance/covariance structure before applying GLS.

scenes.title: Derive GLS from the covariance matrix
scenes.objective: Understand the matrix weighting in GLS.

blocks.p: For y=Xβ+u, suppose E(u|X)=0 and Var(u|X)=Ω, where Ω is known and positive definite. The GLS estimator minimizes the weighted quadratic form (y−Xβ)′Ω⁻¹(y−Xβ).
Differentiating the quadratic form and setting the normal equations to zero gives β̂_GLS=(X′Ω⁻¹X)⁻¹X′Ω⁻¹y, assuming X′Ω⁻¹X is invertible.
Choose C such that C′C=Ω⁻¹. Then Cy=CXβ+Cu and Var(Cu|X)=I. Applying OLS to the transformed model is GLS.

ask.q: What matrix determines the GLS weights?
ask.nudge: It is the inverse of the disturbance covariance matrix.

scenes.title: Worked example: diagonal WLS weights
scenes.objective: Transform a model with known unequal variances.
scenes.problem: Suppose Var(uᵢ|X)=σ²hᵢ, with h=(1,4,9). What row multipliers transform the model to unit error variance, and what WLS weights result?

steps.say: Divide observation i by the square root of hᵢ.
steps.why: The transformed error variance is σ²hᵢ/hᵢ=σ².

steps.say: The row multipliers are inverse standard deviations.
steps.why: These are the factors applied to yᵢ and the corresponding row of X.

steps.say: The least-squares criterion is weighted by inverse hᵢ.
steps.why: Squaring the row multipliers produces weights 1, 1/4 and 1/9.

ask.q: What are the three relative WLS weights?
ask.nudge: Use inverse h, not inverse square-root h.

scenes.title: Guided problem: compute a GLS estimate
scenes.objective: Apply the GLS formula to a diagonal covariance.
scenes.problem: Let X=(1,1)′, y=(2,4)′ and Ω=diag(1,4). Find the GLS estimate of the scalar β in yᵢ=β+uᵢ.
solution: The numerator is X′Ω⁻¹y=2+1=3; the denominator is X′Ω⁻¹X=1+1/4=1.25.
Therefore β̂_GLS=3/1.25=2.4. The second observation receives one-quarter of the first observation's weight.

ask.nudge: The second observation has variance four times as large.

scenes.title: Feasible GLS and robust covariance
scenes.objective: Distinguish estimated weighting from robust standard errors.

blocks.p: When Ω is unknown, specify a variance model, estimate its parameters, construct Ω̂, and substitute Ω̂⁻¹ into the GLS formula. This is feasible GLS (FGLS). Its quality depends on the variance model and the accuracy of Ω̂.
A heteroscedasticity-consistent sandwich estimator keeps β̂_OLS but replaces the conventional covariance estimate. In a common HC form it is (X′X)⁻¹[Σ xᵢxᵢ′ êᵢ²](X′X)⁻¹, with finite-sample variants.

Use robust SEs when the primary need is inference robust to unknown heteroscedasticity. Consider WLS/FGLS when the variance structure is substantively defensible and efficiency matters. Compare results and avoid treating estimated weights as known truth.

ask.q: Do robust standard errors change the OLS coefficient estimates?
ask.nudge: They change the estimated uncertainty around the same coefficients.

scenes.title: Guided problem: choose the method
scenes.objective: Select a defensible correction for each situation.
scenes.problem: A cross-sectional study has a plausible zero conditional mean but unknown heteroscedasticity. No reliable variance function is available. What is the sensible first inference adjustment?
hints: The target is inference for the OLS conditional-mean coefficients.
The variance function is unknown and not credibly modelled.
Choose a method that does not require estimating a full variance model.
scenes.answer: Use heteroscedasticity-robust (sandwich) standard errors for OLS inference.
solution: Retain the OLS coefficient estimates under the maintained mean/exogeneity assumptions.
Replace conventional standard errors with a heteroscedasticity-consistent covariance estimator.
State that this does not repair endogeneity or misspecification of the conditional mean.

ask.q: What important limitation should accompany this recommendation?
ask.nudge: Robust SEs do not repair a biased coefficient estimator.

scenes.title: Exam traps and method distinctions
scenes.objective: Avoid common false claims about heteroscedasticity.
scenes.intro: Check each statement against the exact assumption it concerns.

items.claim: Heteroscedasticity necessarily makes OLS coefficients biased.
items.why: Under exogeneity, OLS may remain unbiased/consistent; variance and efficiency are affected.

items.claim: Conventional homoscedastic OLS standard errors are generally valid under heteroscedasticity.
items.why: Use a heteroscedasticity-consistent covariance estimate or a valid variance model.

items.claim: For Var(uᵢ|X)=σ²hᵢ, the WLS weight is 1/hᵢ.
items.why: The row multiplier is 1/√hᵢ, whose square gives the criterion weight.

items.claim: FGLS treats the estimated covariance matrix as if it were known without uncertainty.
items.why: The covariance is estimated; its quality and finite-sample uncertainty matter.

scenes.title: Summary: what to remember
scenes.objective: Consolidate the path from diagnosis to correction.
body: Heteroscedasticity is non-constant conditional error variance. It does not, by itself, imply a nonzero conditional mean or biased OLS coefficients.
The conventional OLS covariance formula is generally wrong under heteroscedasticity, and OLS is generally inefficient among linear unbiased estimators.
Robust standard errors support inference without changing OLS coefficients. GLS uses Ω⁻¹; WLS is its diagonal special case. FGLS estimates the variance structure first.
For Var(uᵢ|X)=σ²hᵢ, divide row i by √hᵢ and use weight 1/hᵢ. Always state the assumptions behind the chosen correction.

ask.q: In one line, distinguish robust SE from WLS.
ask.nudge: One changes estimated uncertainty; the other changes the fitting criterion.
